transcript.content:
Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Lagos, Nigeria at 2026-01-20 11:57 WAT (UTC+0100) (2026-01-20T10:57:00Z in UTC), at latitude 6.5244 degrees and longitude 3.3792 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 59.542 degrees and its azimuth is 151.107 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 47.814 degrees and its azimuth is 124.404 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 2.74 percent illuminated, 19.022 degrees from the Sun, and 385267.8 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Probably not—at least not reliably with the unaided eye.

Although the Moon is high enough above the horizon (about 48°) and the sky is clear, the decisive issue is its very small elongation from the Sun: only about 19°. At just 2.7% illuminated, it is an extremely thin young crescent sitting in bright daytime sky, only roughly 19° away from the Sun’s glare. The Sun is also very high, so the surrounding sky will be intensely bright.

A skilled, prepared observer might possibly glimpse it under exceptional transparency if they know the exact position and carefully block the Sun behind a building, pole, or their hand. But for an ordinary observer—even one looking in approximately the right area—the odds are low. It would likely be invisible unless you had optical aid or unusually favorable conditions.

Do not use binoculars or a telescope anywhere near the Sun unless you are absolutely certain the Sun cannot enter the field of view; accidental solar viewing can cause permanent eye damage.
